quote: Warscheinlich ist dazu nur eine einzige Bedingung für die Coefficienten der $\Phi_i$ zu erfüllen nöthig.
english: Probably only a single condition on the coefficients of the Φ_i needs to be satisfied for this.
topic: Hilbert sketches how to vary the coefficients of the Φ_i so that x−α stays an inessential divisor of the discriminant, aiming to show that arbitrary branch points can be prescribed and complicated branch points obtained by coalescing simple ones, and starts a proof of the functional-determinant theorem used for this.

triage.modern_statement: Here is my reading of the note. Take an algebraic function y(x) defined by F(x,y)=0, with coefficients built from the Φ_i. Suppose the discriminant of F with respect to y has a factor x−α that is 'inessential' (außerwesentlich): the polynomial discriminant vanishes at α, but the field (function-field) discriminant does not. Geometrically, the curve has a singular point over x=α, such as a node, but the covering x: C → P^1 is not branched there. Hilbert guesses that keeping x−α inessential while the coefficients vary takes only one equation on the coefficients, i.e. a codimension-one condition. In modern terms: in the parameter space of the equations, the curves with a singularity over the discriminant root (one node) form a divisor. Hilbert wants this to show that any branch points can be prescribed, and that complicated branch points come from merging simple ones. That is the classical Riemann existence / Clebsch–Hurwitz setting of Hurwitz spaces of covers.
triage.answered_by: No one answered Hilbert's note directly. The underlying fact became standard algebraic geometry. In the Severi-variety theory of nodal plane curves (Severi, later Harris), curves with one node form a divisor, so one node is one condition. Clebsch (1872) and Hurwitz (1891) built Hurwitz spaces of covers with simple branch points and proved they are connected; a degeneration argument then gets other branch types by merging simple branch points. I found no source that discusses this diary entry itself.

evidence.claim: This survey says the closure of the locus of plane curves of degree d with a node at a given point p is a divisor in the closed Severi variety. The same locus has codimension 3 in the full linear system |dH|. So 'one condition' holds only if the singular point may move; if the point is fixed, more conditions are needed.
This paper says Severi and other Italian geometers already studied varieties of plane curves with a fixed number of nodes and cusps, and how nice (T-smooth) those varieties are.
Hurwitz spaces first appeared in work by Clebsch (1872) and Hurwitz (1891).
Over a century ago, Clebsch and Hurwitz proved that the space of covers with simple branching is connected. Classifying the connected components of Hurwitz spaces in general is still studied.

A recent paper studies when Hurwitz spaces with one prescribed branch point plus enough simple branch points are irreducible. This is the modern version of getting complicated branching by degenerating simple branching.

triage.why: The note is a short working guess inside a proof sketch, not a stated problem. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Read as 'keeping one non-branching discriminant factor (a node) is a codimension-one condition', it agrees with standard results on Severi varieties. That only works if α moves with the coefficients; with α fixed, the count is different. The goal it serves, prescribing branch points and getting complicated ones from simple ones, is the classical Riemann existence and Clebsch–Hurwitz theory, which is settled. Connectivity and irreducibility of Hurwitz and Severi varieties are still active research areas. I can't tell exactly what Hilbert meant (what the Φ_i are, or whether α is fixed), and I found no source on this specific entry, so the match is my interpretation, not a documented answer.
